content: The term heart disease encompasses a variety of conditions that affect the heart. The most prevalent form of heart disease in the United States is coronary artery disease (CAD), which impairs blood flow to the heart. Reduced blood flow due to CAD can lead to a heart attack. Heart disease can sometimes remain silent, meaning it may not be diagnosed until a person experiences significant events such as a heart attack, heart failure, or an arrhythmia. When these events occur, the symptoms can vary: Heart attack symptoms may include chest pain or discomfort, pain in the upper back or neck, sensations similar to heartburn, nausea or vomiting, extreme fatigue, dizziness, and shortness of breath. Arrhythmias may present as fluttering sensations in the chest, often described as palpitations. Heart failure symptoms can include shortness of breath, fatigue, and swelling in areas such as the feet, ankles, legs, abdomen, or neck veins. Several factors increase the risk of developing heart disease. The primary risk factors include high blood pressure, high blood cholesterol, and smoking. Approximately 47% of adults in the United States have at least one of these three risk factors. Additional medical conditions and lifestyle choices that elevate the risk of heart disease include diabetes, being overweight or obese, consuming an unhealthy diet, physical inactivity, and excessive alcohol consumption. Mental health disorders may also have a connection to heart disease. In 2022, heart disease was responsible for 702,880 deaths in the United States, accounting for 1 in every 5 deaths. For individuals recovering from a heart attack, heart failure, or certain types of heart surgery, cardiac rehabilitation is a critical component of treatment and recovery. This structured program is supervised and includes several key elements: Physical activity tailored to the individual’s condition. Education on adopting a heart-healthy diet. Guidance on adhering to prescribed medications. Support for smoking cessation. Counseling to manage stress and improve mental health. A multidisciplinary team typically oversees cardiac rehabilitation. This team may include healthcare providers, exercise and nutrition specialists, physical therapists, and mental health professionals or counselors. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) is actively involved in initiatives to combat heart disease, such as the Million Hearts® program and the WISEWOMAN program. These efforts aim to reduce the prevalence of heart disease and improve cardiovascular health across the population.
